title: Testing an Organ Outside the Body
endLine: Isolate a tissue to control its bath and test one cause.

scenes.tts: When a blood vessel widens in the body, what made it relax? Nerves, hormones, wall stretch, and local chemicals all pull on it at once. To test one signal cleanly, physiologists take a living piece of tissue out of the body.
scenes.caption: When a blood vessel widens in the body, what made it relax? Nerves, hormones, wall stretch, and local chemicals all pull on it at once. To test one signal cleanly, physiologists take a living piece of tissue out of the body.
scenes.visual: A schematic body outline fills the frame around one blood vessel; four labelled arrows (nerves, hormones, stretch, local chemicals) pulse on the vessel at once as it widens beside a question mark, then a cut ring of the vessel lifts cleanly out of the body (schematic).
scenes.narration: When a blood vessel widens in the body, what made it relax? Nerves, hormones, wall stretch, and local chemicals all pull on it at once. To test one signal cleanly, physiologists take a living piece of tissue out of the body.

scenes.visual: The schematic body dissolves while the cut vessel ring settles inside a clear glass organ bath filling most of the frame height, with gently rising bubbles; the title 'Testing an Organ Outside the Body' appears cleanly above the bath (schematic).

scenes.tts: They mount that cut ring of blood vessel inside a glass chamber called an organ bath. Nerves and circulating hormones are now gone. The experimenter controls the fluid around the ring, the load stretching it, and every chemical dripped in. A trace shows whether the ring pulls tighter or relaxes.
scenes.caption: They mount that cut ring of blood vessel inside a glass chamber called an organ bath. Nerves and circulating hormones are now gone. scenes.visual: The vessel ring hangs on two fine supports inside the gently bubbling glass organ bath; crossed-out nerve and hormone icons fade away; bath fluid, a gentle stretching load, and a dropper above light up one by one as a live schematic tension trace draws on the right (schematic).
scenes.narration: They mount that cut ring of blood vessel inside a glass chamber called an organ bath. Nerves and circulating hormones are now gone. The experimenter controls the fluid around the ring, the load stretching it, and every chemical dripped in. A trace shows whether the ring pulls tighter or relaxes.

scenes.tts: Every vessel has a single-cell inner lining called the endothelium, sitting over smooth muscle. Drip acetylcholine into the bath around an intact ring, and the ring relaxes. That illustrates the method's guiding idea. Remove a living tissue to control its bath and test one cause at a time.

scenes.visual: Closer view of the same vessel ring in the bubbling bath: its thin inner lining ('endothelium') lights up before the outer layer ('smooth muscle'); the dropper releases schematic acetylcholine dots into the bath, the ring widens, and the schematic tension trace drops (schematic).
scenes.narration: Every vessel has a single-cell inner lining called the endothelium, sitting over smooth muscle. Drip acetylcholine into the bath around an intact ring, and the ring relaxes. That illustrates the method's guiding idea. Remove a living tissue to control its bath and test one cause at a time.

scenes.tts: Now change just one part in the same bath. Gently rub off that thin inner lining, leaving the smooth muscle wall behind. Drip acetylcholine in again. Predict what happens: does the ring still relax?
scenes.caption: Now change just one part in the same bath. Gently rub off that thin inner lining, leaving the smooth muscle wall behind. Drip acetylcholine in again. Predict what happens: does the ring still relax?
scenes.visual: In the same bubbling organ bath, the inner lining peels away from the vessel ring while the smooth muscle wall stays mounted; the dropper poises above with schematic acetylcholine dots and the question 'Does the ring still relax?' appears cleanly (schematic).
scenes.narration: Now change just one part in the same bath. Gently rub off that thin inner lining, leaving the smooth muscle wall behind. Drip acetylcholine in again. Predict what happens: does the ring still relax?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause: the rubbed ring sits in the gently bubbling bath as schematic acetylcholine dots drift around it; the schematic tension trace pauses at a pulsing question mark while 'Does the ring still relax?' stays on screen (schematic).

scenes.tts: No, without its lining, the ring stays tight. Acetylcholine does not relax smooth muscle directly. It acts on endothelial cells, which make nitric oxide. Small and uncharged, nitric oxide crosses freely into neighboring smooth muscle and relaxes it. Comparing intact and rubbed rings exposed the messenger; later work showed it was nitric oxide.

scenes.visual: The schematic tension trace stays flat on the rubbed ring; intact and rubbed rings then appear side by side in twin glass baths — on the intact ring, schematic acetylcholine dots touch the endothelium, small nitric oxide dots cross into the smooth muscle, and that ring widens while the rubbed ring stays tight (schematic).
scenes.narration: No, without its lining, the ring stays tight. Acetylcholine does not relax smooth muscle directly. It acts on endothelial cells, which make nitric oxide. Small and uncharged, nitric oxide crosses freely into neighboring smooth muscle and relaxes it. Comparing intact and rubbed rings exposed the messenger; later work showed it was nitric oxide.

scenes.tts: Still, an isolated bath can mislead you. In a frog nerve and muscle, temperature follows surroundings, and cooling slows conduction. So a room-temperature frog value is not a human value at thirty-seven degrees Celsius. Nerve speed is distance over nerve delay, so first subtract junction and muscle delays. Guard against mistakes with matched controls, subtracted delays, and species checks.

So a room-temperature frog value is not a human value at 37 °C. Nerve speed is distance over nerve delay, so first subtract junction and muscle delays. Guard against mistakes with matched controls, subtracted delays, and species checks.
scenes.visual: The same glass bath now holds a schematic frog nerve joined to a muscle; a schematic bath thermometer drops from 37 °C to room temperature and a glowing impulse slows along the nerve; on the right, a schematic timing bar shows junction and muscle delay being subtracted from the total delay (schematic).

Guard against mistakes with matched controls, subtracted delays, and species checks.

scenes.tts: With controls like those, isolated preparations unlocked major discoveries. In 1980, Robert Furchgott and John Zawadzki ran that exact organ-bath test on rabbit aortic rings. Only intact rings relaxed to acetylcholine, showing that the lining sends a signal to the muscle beneath.
scenes.caption: With controls like those, isolated preparations unlocked major discoveries. In 1980, Robert Furchgott and John Zawadzki ran that exact organ-bath test on rabbit aortic rings. Only intact rings relaxed to acetylcholine, showing that the lining sends a signal to the muscle beneath.
scenes.visual: In the glass organ bath, intact and rubbed rabbit aortic rings reappear side by side under a clean '1980 — Furchgott & Zawadzki' label; schematic acetylcholine relaxes only the intact ring as a signal arrow moves from endothelium to smooth muscle (schematic).
scenes.narration: With controls like those, isolated preparations unlocked major discoveries. In 1980, Robert Furchgott and John Zawadzki ran that exact organ-bath test on rabbit aortic rings. Only intact rings relaxed to acetylcholine, showing that the lining sends a signal to the muscle beneath.

scenes.tts: In 1970, Kokko held tiny rabbit kidney tubules, thin descending limbs, between glass pipettes. He flowed controlled fluid through the inside while setting the bath outside. That isolated perfused tubule showed low sodium permeability and no detectable active salt transport. Water permeability, though, still varies across species.

scenes.visual: Inside the same glass bath under a '1970 — Kokko' label, the vessel ring transforms into a single thin kidney tubule held between two glass pipettes; schematic fluid flows through the inner channel while bath fluid surrounds it, and almost no sodium dots cross the tubule wall (schematic).

scenes.tts: And Dale and Feldberg solved a speed problem. An enzyme called acetylcholinesterase clears acetylcholine from the nerve-muscle gap in milliseconds. They blocked that enzyme and used a living muscle as a detector to catch it. Strip away competing body signals, keep the tissue alive, and one controlled test can reveal the cause.

scenes.visual: Inside the glass bath under a 'Dale & Feldberg' label, schematic acetylcholine dots vanish rapidly in a nerve-muscle gap until schematic blockers halt clearance and the living muscle contracts on the trace; the bath then holds vessel ring, tubule, and muscle gently bubbling together (schematic).
